strengths: The paper addresses a timely and security-relevant problem: training-time steganographic exfiltration in LLMs, building directly on TrojanStego (Meier et al., 2025) and improving it along a well-motivated axis (recoverability vs. attack effectiveness).

The formalization of payload recoverability along two axes (Rbucket and Rsecret) via keyless classifier accuracy is a useful conceptual contribution that reframes how steganographic channel strength should be measured for fine-tuning-based attacks, and the empirical demonstration that TrojanStego is perfectly recoverable on both axes is convincing (Figure 2).

The embedding-space hyperplane encoding/bucketing schemes are a sensible design, and the experimental matrix is extensive: three models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full and LoRA fine-tuning, two datasets, ablations of encoding vs. bucketing components, OOD prompt generalization, and text-quality metrics (coherence, stability, perplexity, KL). The results showing accuracy gains (up to +123% on Llama-70B LoRA) combined with reduced recoverability are well-supported by Tables 1-2.

The theoretical bounds (Thms 7.1, 7.2) with full KKT-based proofs in the appendix support the argument that standard steganalysis via KL/perplexity is insufficient for this threat model, which is a point that had previously only been argued informally.

The XOR-masking control (Section 7.4, Appendix G) is a thoughtful experimental design element: it decouples mechanistic detectability from output-side payload recoverability, and the finding that detection persists in a non-decodable setting strengthens the central detection claim.

The paper is honest about limitations: white-box detection assumption, failed detection scenarios (Table 3, bit accuracy succeeds in only 3/8 XOR cases), occasional accuracy underperformances, and an appropriate impact statement with responsible disclosure plans.
weaknesses: The 'low-recoverability' claim is only relative to a small, fixed family of keyless classifiers (XGBoost and 2-layer MLPs, Appendix C). Definition 3.1 quantifies over families H and G but the paper provides no evidence that stronger or differently structured adversaries (e.g., hyperplane-fitting attacks, seed recovery, larger MLPs, or the explicit seed-recovery methods cited in Section 5.2) also fail. Calling the schemes 'unrecoverable' or even 'low-recoverability' overstates what is demonstrated; the metric's classifier-family dependence deserves more discussion.

The detection analysis lacks a crucial control: a benignly fine-tuned model (e.g., fine-tuned on the identical data without bucket constraints, or on matched generic data). Since the secret appears in plaintext in training prompts, any fine-tuned model may expose prompt content in activations, and the probe gap (fine-tuned vs. base) could partly reflect generic fine-tuning effects or prompt memorization rather than a steganography-specific signature. Without this baseline, the 'mechanistic detection signal' contribution is not fully established.

The headline '33% higher accuracy' detection claim is loosely derived: Figure 5 shows fine-tuned probes reaching 95-100% vs. base ~60% at the final layer, but detection success is inconsistent (embedding regression is 'less pronounced'; Ministral-8B full fine-tuning shows unclear separation; XOR bit detection succeeds in only 3/8 scenarios), and cosine-similarity-based embedding recovery is harder to translate into a concrete defender decision procedure.

The theoretical contribution is modest: both theorems are lower bounds under idealized assumptions (peaked two-token distributions, uniform bucket assignment, argmax promotion only), and the numerical example (0.026 nats) is illustrative rather than grounded in realistic next-token distributions. The bounds bound a best-case adversary's distributional footprint, which supports the argument but is far from a complete steganalysis-insufficiency result.

Practical significance of the threat model is narrow: 4-letter secrets (32 bits), constrained generation only at payload positions, single-bit-per-token channels, and the detection method requiring hidden-state access (acknowledged in the conclusion). The gap between the demonstrated capability and real exfiltration scenarios is not deeply analyzed.

Some experimental results are under-explained: OOD generalization varies erratically across configurations (Table 2, e.g., W-trained models at 0-5% on T prompts vs. 39-45% on G prompts), and the paper attributes this qualitatively to 'prompt structure interacting with hyperparameters' without a rigorous analysis; several ablations (E+E T on Ministral Full) underperform with limited diagnosis.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored gap: prior training-time steganography (TrojanStego) is trivially keyless-recoverable, and framing 'payload recoverability' as a complement to statistical detectability is a reasonable and useful distinction for this threat model.

The XOR-masking control (Section 7.4, Appendix G) is a well-conceived experimental control that decouples mechanistic detectability from output-side decodability, which is the right way to test the central claim that internal signatures persist even when the payload is non-decodable.

The evaluation is fairly broad along several axes: three models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full vs. LoRA fine-tuning, two training-data distributions, OOD prompt generalization, and four text-quality metrics, with ablations across encoding/bucketing combinations.

The KL and perplexity lower-bound analysis (Theorems 7.1 and 7.2) provides a clean, if simple, argument for why distributional steganalysis has limited power against fine-tuning-based channels, and the proofs in Appendix B appear correct.

An honest limitations discussion and impact statement, including acknowledgment that detection requires hidden-state access and that future training setups may evade linear probes, with a responsible-disclosure plan for attack code.
weaknesses: The recoverability formalization (Definition 3.1) is only as strong as the chosen classifier families (XGBoost and small MLPs). Claiming a scheme is 'low-recoverability' because these particular keyless classifiers fail is weak evidence: a motivated defender with white-box access to the deployed model could search the seed space directly (the bucketing uses a single seed, so the search space for beta_sigma is tiny once seeds are guessed), and the paper itself cites seed-recovery work (Tong et al., 2025) without quantifying resistance to it. R_bucket would likely be near 1 under a seed-search adversary, undermining the headline 'low-recoverability' claim.

The mechanistic detection result is largely expected by construction, not a surprising finding. Because the bucketing scheme is implemented via frozen embeddings plus a fixed hyperplane, the fine-tuned model must internally compute bucket assignments to satisfy the channel, so it is nearly tautological that late-layer activations linearly encode the bits. The '33% higher accuracy' framing overstates the significance of what is essentially a sanity check that the mechanism is implemented in the model.

Detection results are inconsistent and incomplete: under the XOR-masking control, bit-accuracy detection succeeds in only 3 of 8 scenarios, and full fine-tuning of Ministral-8B yields unclear separation in both Figure 5 and Table 3. The defense contribution therefore does not hold reliably across the very settings the paper introduces, weakening the claim that 'steganographic exfiltration is detectable from internal signatures alone.'

The attack's practical value is questionable: exact-match rates of 30% (Llama-8B LoRA), 43% (Ministral-8B LoRA), and 19% (Llama-70B) mean the channel frequently fails to transmit a 32-bit secret even in distribution, and OOD generalization collapses for many configurations (e.g., near-0% on Wiki prompts for several T-trained models in Table 2). Relative improvements (+78%, +123%) are over low baselines; a covert channel that drops most of its payload is a weak attack regardless of recoverability.

The theoretical bounds are loose and weakly connected to the empirical claims: Theorem 7.2 only lower-bounds perplexity by ~2, and the numerical KL example relies on hand-picked distributional assumptions (p1=0.5, p2=0.3). The bridge from these bounds to 'within typical fine-tuning ranges' rests on citing Rafailov et al. (2023) rather than a rigorous comparison.

Some experimental design choices reduce confidence: a single bucketing seed (sigma=42) is used throughout Section D.1, so no evidence is given that results generalize across seeds; text-quality metrics are computed on only 10-20 prompts per configuration, making the Figure 4 comparisons noisy; and base models already reach ~60% bit-probe accuracy, indicating the secret (present in plaintext in the prompt) leaks into activations of benign models too, complicating the interpretation of the detection gap.

Originality is incremental: the core attack mechanics (bucket-constrained generation during fine-tuning) are taken from Meier et al. (2025), and the contribution reduces to swapping ASCII/parity for hyperplane-based encoding/bucketing plus applying standard linear-probe methodology. The combination is reasonable but not a substantial conceptual advance.

Presentation issues: Table 2 and Figures 4-5 are dense and difficult to parse; results are reported as relative improvements over low absolute numbers, which can mislead; and key caveats (e.g., that R_bucket is defined only over two classifier families, or that detection under the unrecoverable control is inconsistent) are not surfaced prominently enough relative to the abstract's claims.

strengths: Meaningful problem framing: the paper identifies a real gap in TrojanStego (trivially recoverable encoding/bucketing) and formalizes payload recoverability along two complementary axes (Rbucket and Rsecret), which is a useful conceptual contribution for LLM steganalysis.

The attack-side method is technically sound and well-motivated: seed-dependent random hyperplanes in embedding space are a natural way to couple the covert channel to the model's learned geometry, making the channel easier for the model to learn while harder to reverse-engineer without the key.

Comprehensive attack evaluation: three models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full and LoRA fine-tuning, two training datasets, four encoding/bucketing combinations, and OOD prompt generalization tests with a well-designed ablation that cleanly attributes most gains to the bucketing scheme (ASCII+Embedding performs best).

The detection-side analysis is the most original part: the KL and perplexity lower-bound theorems (with detailed KKT-based proofs in the appendix) make a convincing theoretical case that standard distributional steganalysis is fundamentally limited for fine-tuning-based attacks, and the XOR-masking control (Section 7.4) cleverly decouples mechanistic detection from output-side decodability.

OOD prompt evaluation for the probes, careful probe methodology details (layer choice, feature scaling, CI calculation), and an honest treatment of limitations (white-box/gray-box assumptions, Ministral full fine-tuning being harder to detect, detection failing in some XOR scenarios).
Responsible dual-use treatment: impact statement, promise of detection code release, and coordination with model providers for attack disclosure.
weaknesses: The central 'low-recoverability' claim is only partially supported. Rbucket and Rsecret are defined as a max over a small, fixed family of classifiers (XGBoost/MLP); a motivated keyless analyst who suspects hyperplane bucketing could brute-force or estimate the seed orientation from many samples, and the paper does not quantify how many samples the defender needs or report the actual Rbucket/Rsecret values for the embedding schemes (Figure 2 is hard to read and the exact values in the 'Embedding Bucketing' region are not stated numerically).

The linear-probe detection results have an unexplained anomaly: base models achieve ~60% bit-prediction accuracy, well above the stated 50% chance baseline, despite unconstrained greedy decoding in which base models encode no secret. Without understanding what the base-model probes are picking up, the magnitude and interpretation of the 'up to 33% higher accuracy' detection gap are unclear.

Only a single bucketing seed (sigma=42) is used for the main experiments, so the paper does not show robustness of either attack learning or defense detection across the seed distribution; the 'requires access to hidden seeds' security argument would be more convincing with multi-seed experiments.

Detection requires white-box/gray-box access to hidden states at known token positions, which substantially limits practical applicability to deployed-model auditing; the paper acknowledges this but it reduces the significance of the defense contribution relative to its framing.

Some evidential inconsistencies are not fully resolved: Embedding+Embedding fails to show the detection divergence pattern in Figure 5, bit detection succeeds in only 3 of 8 XOR scenarios, and several OOD/underperformance cases (e.g., E+E T on Ministral) are mentioned but not analyzed.

Theoretical bounds, while correctly derived, largely formalize the intuitive point that constrained generation requires only bounded distribution shift; the numerical example relies on simplified assumptions (two-token peaked distribution, uniform buckets) that may not reflect real model geometry.

Presentation issues: Table 1's dense abbreviations (W/T, five model columns) are hard to parse, Figure 4's bar charts are cramped and hard to read, and notation around Ltx (32 vs. 128 repeated-cycle setup) requires careful tracking across sections.

strengths: The paper formalizes payload recoverability along two complementary axes (R_bucket and R_secret) using keyless classifiers, which is a genuinely useful diagnostic for LLM covert channels and cleanly demonstrates that TrojanStego's ASCII+parity scheme is trivially recoverable (R=1 on both axes).

The embedding-space hyperplane encoding/bucketing scheme is a sensible, well-motivated design: it improves exact-match accuracy across models (e.g., 17→30%, 9→19% relative to baseline) while lowering recoverability, and the ablation grid (E+E, A+E, E+P vs A+P) isolates where the gains come from.

The empirical study is unusually thorough: full vs LoRA fine-tuning, three models including a 70B setting, OOD prompt generalization, capability benchmarks, text quality metrics, decoding-temperature robustness, retokenization/bucket-flip analysis (Appendix H), and mixed-motive training to restore capability while preserving the channel.

The XOR-masking control (Section 7.5) is a thoughtful experimental design that decouples mechanistic detectability from output-side decodability, showing detection signals persist even when the payload is non-decodable.

The theoretical KL and perplexity bounds (Theorems 7.1, 7.2), while simple, are correctly derived via KKT conditions and give quantitative support to the claim that standard steganalysis is insufficient for fine-tuning-based attacks.
Honest, detailed limitations section covering threat-model assumptions, capability degradation, hyperplane-search scaling, and the white-box detection requirement.
weaknesses: The recoverability metric is defined as a max over a fixed, small classifier family (XGBoost and shallow MLPs). Claiming a scheme is 'unrecoverable' or has low recoverability depends entirely on this family; no adaptive attack (e.g., a stronger learned decoder or hyperplane recovery attack à la Tong et al., 2025) is actually attempted, so the key security claim rests on the weakness of the assumed adversary.

The attack's practical significance is limited: exact-match rates remain modest (17–43%), secrets are only 4 letters / 32 bits, and full fine-tuning causes 20–33 pp capability degradation; mixed-motive training restores capability only partially and inconsistently (Ministral Full still loses ~20 pp).

The detection contribution assumes white-box access to hidden states and probes trained with knowledge of bit positions or secret embeddings (for the regression variant, PCA targets of secret letters); the paper itself acknowledges in the limitations that output-only/black-box detection remains open, and that future adversary training could evade linear probes — so the defense is narrow relative to the framing.

The detection claim 'up to 33% higher accuracy' is a cherry-picked best case; several configurations (e.g., Embedding+Embedding bit classification, Ministral full fine-tuning, bit accuracy under XOR masking succeeding in only 3 of 8 scenarios) show weaker separation, and the paper's summary language overstates uniformity.

Some writing quality issues suggest draft-level polish problems: Section 6.1 states 'we will also develop mixed motive data... We will motivate this dataset more deeply as the section progresses' (future tense promises in a results paper), and there are minor inconsistencies (e.g., text says Appendix Table 7 where Table 8 is meant in H.2).

The perplexity/KL bounds, while correct, largely formalize the intuitive observation that constrained generation can be low-KL; their connection to the specific empirical attack is loose (the attack uses 1 bit/token, not the 10-bit/1024-bucket setting analyzed).

Ethical handling is reasonable (dual-use statement, responsible disclosure plan for attack code) but the attack contribution itself (improved covert exfiltration) provides a ready recipe that may lower the barrier for malicious fine-tuning; the defense component mitigates but does not eliminate this concern.

strengths: Well-motivated dual attack/defense framing: the paper both strengthens a training-time steganographic channel (building on TrojanStego, Meier et al. 2025) and studies its detectability, which is a coherent research program.

The formalization of payload recoverability along two axes (R_bucket and R_secret via keyless classifier accuracy) is a sensible and underexplored diagnostic that usefully separates 'detectability' from 'payload extraction' (Sec. 3, drawing on Fridrich & Kodovský 2012).

Substantial empirical scope: three models (Llama-8B, Ministral-8B, Llama-70B), full fine-tuning and LoRA, multiple encodings/bucketings, three datasets, OOD generalization, capability benchmarks (MMLU/ARC/HellaSwag/WinoGrande), and text-quality metrics.

The theoretical KL-divergence and perplexity bounds (Thms 7.1, 7.2, with KKT proofs in Appendix B) are correct and give a clean argument for why perplexity/KL-based steganalysis is insufficient under fine-tuning drift.

The secret-conditioned XOR-masking control (Sec. 7.5, App. G) is a clever design that decouples mechanistic detection from output-side decodability, and the honest reporting of its partial failure (bit detection succeeds in only 3 of 8 scenarios, Table 4) is commendable.

Honest limitations section (App. I) covering threat-model assumptions, capability degradation, hyperplane-search scaling, and the white-box nature of the detection method; responsible disclosure plan is stated.
weaknesses: The central 'low-recoverability' claim conflates computational hardness with recoverability. The bucketing rule is fully deterministic given the seed; R_bucket/R_secret are measured only against a small, fixed family of classifiers (XGBoost/MLP, App. C) with limited samples. A stronger adaptive attacker (seed search, Tong et al. 2025 which the authors themselves cite, or simply more output samples) is not evaluated, so 'unrecoverable' (R_bucket ≈ 50%) is not well supported as a property of the scheme, only of the tested attacker.

No benign-fine-tuning control for the detection results. The mechanistic claim rests on comparing probes on steganographically fine-tuned models vs. *base* models. Any fine-tuning (benign or malicious) can change what linear probes extract; without a matched benign SFT control (e.g., the 25% instruction data trained alone), the 'up to 33% higher accuracy' cannot be attributed to steganography specifically rather than to fine-tuning-induced representational changes generally.

Misleading abstract phrasing: 'exact secret recovery rises from 17→30%' describes attack encoding success (exact match), which reads as defender-side recovery. This terminological slippage between attack accuracy and defender recoverability recurs and obscures the actual trade-off being claimed.

The attack contribution is largely incremental relative to TrojanStego: replacing ASCII/parity with hyperplane-derived mappings is a natural substitution, and the paper itself shows most gains come from the bucketing half (E+P gives only ~12% average gain). Some headline gains come from changing the training data/schedule (32 vs 128 constrained tokens, LoRA rank 128 for Wiki), confounding the encoding comparison.

Theoretical bounds are weakly connected to the actual attack: the bounds are for argmax-promotion channels with uniform bucket assignment, while the experiments use a single 2-way hyperplane bucket and empirical KL/PPL numbers are only loosely argued to be 'within typical fine-tuning ranges' (citing Rafailov et al. 2023 without a direct measurement of the benign-fine-tuning range on the same models/data).

Mixed results are under-interpreted: Ministral full fine-tuning degrades >30 pp on capability benchmarks and shows unclear probe separation; OOD generalization is highly erratic across configurations (Table 2), suggesting the results are sensitive to hyperparameters in ways the paper does not fully explain or control.

Presentation issues: forward references like 'We will motivate this dataset more deeply as the section progresses', typos ('intruction'), a cluttered Figure 2 with many overlapping markers, and results tables whose abbreviations require constant cross-referencing reduce readability.

Dual-use tension: the paper improves the attack (higher encoding accuracy, better retokenization robustness per Table 8, temperature robustness) while the defense relies on white-box hidden-state access, which the authors concede does not apply to black-box/API deployments — the practical defensive value for the most realistic threat setting (closed models) is limited.

strengths: Clear and useful problem formalization: decomposing payload recoverability into R_bucket and R_secret with a keyless defender assumption is a sensible reframing, and the empirical demonstration that TrojanStego's parity/ASCII scheme achieves ~100% recoverability on both axes convincingly motivates the work.

The attack method is well-motivated: seed-dependent random hyperplanes in embedding space simultaneously make bucketing easier for the model to learn (improving exact-match accuracy, e.g., 17→30% on Llama-8B LoRA and 9→19% on Llama-70B) and harder for a defender to reverse-engineer, giving a genuine accuracy/recoverability trade-off improvement over the baseline.

Unusually thorough empirical evaluation for this domain: three models across full and LoRA fine-tuning, multiple training datasets, OOD prompt generalization, downstream capability benchmarks (MMLU, ARC, HellaSwag, WinoGrande), text-quality metrics, decoding-temperature robustness, and retokenization/bucket-flip analysis (Appendix H) — the latter is a subtle real-world issue (tokenizer non-injectivity) that most papers in this space ignore.

Good experimental controls on the defense side: the XOR-masking control (Section 7.5) cleanly decouples mechanistic detectability from output-side decodability, and the mixed-motive training setting tests detection under more realistic (non-steganography-only) fine-tuning.

The KL-divergence and perplexity lower bounds (Theorems 7.1, 7.2), while simple, are correctly derived (KKT argument checks out) and concretely support the claim that distributional steganalysis has limited sensitivity for fine-tuning-based channels.

Honest, specific limitations section covering threat-model assumptions, payload-size scaling, hyperplane-search scaling, and the white-box nature of detection; appropriate impact statement with a responsible-disclosure plan for attack code.
weaknesses: The 'unrecoverable'/'low-recoverability' claims are only as strong as the chosen classifier families (XGBoost and small MLPs over token IDs/PCA-reduced embeddings). An adaptive defender could search hyperplane orientations directly, exploit nearest-neighbor structure of token embeddings, or use seed-recovery techniques the authors themselves cite (Tong et al., 2025; Tramèr et al., 2016) — but only a sentence acknowledges this, and no adaptive attack is actually evaluated. Recoverability relative to a stronger adversary remains an open question.

The detection contribution is modest in methodological novelty (linear probes and ridge regression are standard tools) and limited in scope: bit-classification probes assume the defender has reverse-engineered the encoding (white-box), embedding-recovery probes presuppose knowledge of the secret's embedding family, and everything requires hidden-state access, so it applies mainly to open-weight deployments. The authors acknowledge this, but it substantially limits the practical reach of the defense.

Detection results are not uniformly strong: full fine-tuning on Ministral-8B yields unclear separation, bit detection succeeds in only three of eight XOR-masking scenarios (Table 4), and the E+E scheme resists probes — so the central 'internal signatures alone suffice' claim holds only in a subset of configurations and is stated more confidently than the evidence supports.

Absolute attack performance remains modest: exact match rates of ~20–43% with 4-letter secrets mean the channel is unreliable in most configurations, and the payload scale (32 bits) is far from realistic exfiltration volumes; capability degradation of 10–30 pp under single-objective training further weakens the threat's practicality, and the mixed-motive mitigation is inconsistent for full fine-tuning.

The theoretical bounds rely on idealized assumptions (uniform bucket assignment, argmax-promotion structure, a hand-picked peaked distribution for the numeric example) and are used mainly illustratively; the bridge from 'KL/PPL can be small in principle' to 'standard steganalysis is insufficient in practice' is asserted rather than demonstrated with a matched empirical comparison.

Some claims rest on citation rather than measurement, e.g., that observed perplexity/KL increases 'remain within ranges typical of heavy fine-tuning' (Rafailov et al., 2023) — the empirical values in Figure 4 are non-trivially elevated, and the equivalence of those ranges to instruction-fine-tuning baselines is not established within the paper.
